title: The Night Baker of Willow Street
subtitle: A slow sleep story for tonight
about: An invented story about a baker who works through a rainy spring night and then goes home to sleep. Not a true story.
text:
Welcome. This story is invented, and it is meant to be heard slowly. There is nothing to remember, and nothing to work out. If you fall asleep before the end, that is exactly right, and the story will carry on gently without you.

Let your body grow heavy against the mattress. Let your hands rest wherever they fall. Breathe in slowly, through your nose, and breathe out through your mouth, like a long, quiet sigh. Once more. In, and out. Good.

Now picture a small town in early spring, in the hour after midnight. A fine rain has been falling since the evening, so fine that it hardly makes a sound. It beads on the cobblestones, and on the leaves of the lime trees, and on the lids of the dustbins, and every street shines softly in the light of the lamps.

The houses are dark, with their curtains drawn. Behind them, the people of the town are asleep, in deep and ordinary beds, under heavy blankets. A cat walks along a garden wall, takes no notice of the rain, and disappears into the hedge. The whole town is breathing slowly, and the night belongs to the quiet.

At the end of a narrow lane called Willow Street there is one lit window. It is small and square, and its glass is a little steamed, so that the light looks soft and golden, like the inside of a lantern. Above the door hangs a painted wooden sign in the shape of a wheat sheaf. This is the bakery.

The baker is called Tomas Wren. He is a broad, calm man of fifty-eight, with floury forearms, and thick grey eyebrows, and a face that creases easily into a smile. He wears a white apron, a faded blue cap, and a pair of soft felt shoes that make no noise on the old stone floor.

Tomas has been getting up in the middle of the night for thirty-one years. Long ago, it was difficult. Now it is simply the shape of his life, like the bend of a river. He does not think of it as work. He thinks of it as keeping the town company, from the other side of the dark.

He lets himself in through the side door and hangs his wet coat on a peg. The air inside is warm and smells of flour and old wood and yeast. He takes a deep breath, and his shoulders settle. Everything in the bakery is exactly where he left it, and everything is waiting for him.

On the wall hangs a round clock with a cracked white face. It ticks, very slowly, as though it had never been in a hurry. Under the clock is a long wooden table, scrubbed pale by years of work, and on the table stand the tools: a wooden board, a metal scraper, and a heavy bowl the colour of cream.

He lights the oven first. A small orange flame wakes up behind the iron door, and then spreads, and begins to hum. Tomas holds his palm near it for a moment, and feels the warmth rise, and nods. The oven needs time to be ready, and he has time to give it.

While the oven warms, he fetches the flour. The sacks are stacked in the pantry, and each one is as soft and heavy as a sleeping child. He lifts one onto his shoulder with an easy grunt, carries it to the table, and opens it, and a pale cloud rises and drifts away into the lamplight.

He weighs the flour in a brass scale, with its small, polished weights, one after another, placing them on the pan with two fingers. Then he pours the flour into the big bowl, and it falls with a soft, dry, whispering sound, like fine sand running through a glass.

Next comes the water. He fills a jug at the tap, and tests it with his wrist, as one tests the bath of a baby. It must be neither warm nor cool, but exactly in between. He pours it slowly, and the flour darkens and gathers, and slowly begins to become something else.

Then a pinch of salt, and a spoonful of the starter, which he keeps in a glass jar beside the window. The starter is thirty-one years old, as old as his nights in this room. It bubbles gently, and smells of apples and warm bread, and he thanks it quietly, as he does every night.

Now he rolls up his sleeves and begins to knead. He presses the dough with the heel of his hand, folds it over, turns it a quarter turn, and presses again. Press, fold, turn. Press, fold, turn. His movements are slow and even, a rhythm as steady as breathing.

The dough is rough at first, and then smooth. It grows warm under his hands, and it begins to feel alive, as though a very small heart were beating inside it. He leans into it with his whole weight, and then eases off, and leans in again, like a boat rocking at its moorings.

Outside, the rain continues. You can hear it on the window, a soft, patient tapping, so light that it seems to be only one single drop, falling again and again. Tomas does not mind the sound. He has worked beside it for so many years that it has become a kind of friend.

When the dough is ready, he shapes it into a large, round ball, and sets it in the bowl. He covers it with a damp linen cloth, tucking in the corners, as one tucks in a blanket. Then he rests his hand upon it for a moment, and says, quietly, rest well.

Now the dough must rise, and there is nothing to do but wait. This is the part of the night that Tomas loves best. He pulls out a stool, and sits near the oven, and warms his hands. The kettle on the little stove begins to sing, a thin, silvery note.

He makes a pot of tea, with a spoonful of dried chamomile and a thin slice of lemon. He pours it into a thick white mug, and wraps both hands around it. The steam curls up in front of his face, and the warmth spreads slowly from his palms to his wrists to his shoulders.

On the shelf above him sits a small radio, switched off. He never turns it on at night. He prefers the sounds of the bakery: the quiet tick of the clock, the hum of the oven, the soft hiss of the kettle, and the rain, which has not left once since he arrived.

There is a cat in this bakery, too. She is an old, tortoiseshell creature called Pepper, and she sleeps in a basket by the flour bins. She has one torn ear, and a way of sighing in her sleep, as though the dreams she is having are very comfortable ones.

Tomas leans over, and strokes her head with one finger. Pepper opens a single golden eye, looks at him, and closes it again. Her purr starts up, low and rolling, and joins the hum of the oven, until it is hard to tell which sound comes from where.

He drinks his tea slowly, and thinks of nothing in particular. He thinks of a field of wheat in summer, bending in the wind. He thinks of a river, and of a mill with a slow, turning wheel. He thinks of the long chain of hands that brought this flour to his table.

After a while, he rises, and lifts the cloth from the bowl. The dough has grown, round and soft and full, nearly twice its size. He presses a finger gently into it, and the dent fills in slowly, like a footprint in damp sand. It is ready.

He tips the dough onto the floured table, and divides it with the scraper into smaller pieces. Each piece is the size of a loaf, and each one he weighs in his hands, and shapes with a few quiet strokes. He rolls them under his palms until they are smooth, and round, and calm.

He lays the loaves in rows on long wooden boards, dusts them with flour, and cuts a shallow line across each one with a curved blade. The cuts open slightly, like sleepy eyes. When he has finished, there are twenty loaves in four tidy rows, waiting in the lamplight.

The oven is ready now. He opens the heavy iron door, and a wave of dry, golden heat rolls out and brushes his face. He slides the first board in with a long wooden paddle, a smooth push and a small turn, and the loaves settle onto the hot stone, one after another.

He closes the door gently, and sets a small timer made of brass, and then he sits again. Inside the oven, nothing can be seen, but he can hear it all. A faint crackle, a soft sigh, and then, slowly, the first warm smell of bread begins to creep into the room.

It is the most comforting smell in the world. It is sweet and toasty, and a little bit like honey, and a little bit like a warm blanket on a cold morning. It fills the bakery, and drifts under the door, and out into the rain, and along the sleeping lane.

Somewhere in the town, a window is half open, and the smell reaches a small bedroom, where a child is sleeping. The child does not wake. But a smile tugs at the corner of the sleeping mouth, and the child turns over, and burrows deeper beneath the quilt.

Tomas takes the loaves out one by one, with the paddle, and sets them on a long rack to cool. Their crusts are golden brown and crackled, and as they cool they sing, a thin, delicate crackling, like tiny bells. He listens, and smiles, because it is his favourite sound.

He loads the second board, and the third, and the fourth. The clock ticks on, and the rain taps on the glass, and the bakery grows warmer and warmer, until the windows are completely clouded and the whole room glows like the inside of a small golden shell.

When the last of the bread has cooled, he lines the loaves along the shelves in the front of the shop. They sit shoulder to shoulder, round and plain and handsome, ready for the morning. The people of the town will come for them soon, and they will go home with warm hands.

But that is not yet. Tomas sweeps the floor with a soft broom, in long, slow strokes. He wipes the table, and folds the linen cloth, and hangs it over the rail to dry. He rinses the mug, and sets it upside down on a towel, and everything is quiet and clean.

He checks the oven one last time. It is slowly cooling now, its flame low, its iron door ticking softly as it shrinks. He rests his palm against it, and thanks it, as he thanks the starter, and the cat, and the clock. Then he puts out the lamp over the table.

The bakery is lit only by the glow of the oven, a deep, quiet orange, and by the pale blue of the window, where the first thin hint of dawn is beginning. The rain has softened to almost nothing. The lane outside is silver, and still, and smells of wet stone.

Tomas unties his apron, and folds it, and lays it on the chair. He takes his coat from its peg, and it is dry now, warm from the oven. He slips it on, and pulls his blue cap down over his ears, and Pepper stirs in her basket, and sighs, and settles again.

He steps out through the side door, and locks it with his old brass key. The air is cool and fresh, and it smells of rain and blossom. Somewhere in the hedge, a single bird has begun to sing, a few tentative notes, and then silence, as though it were testing the morning.

He walks home along Willow Street, slowly, with his hands in his pockets. Water drips from the lime trees, one drop at a time, onto the cobblestones. The lamps are going pale in the growing light, and the sky above the rooftops is the colour of the inside of a pearl.

His house is small, and yellow, with a green door and a window box full of crocuses. He lets himself in, and the hall is warm, and smells faintly of soap. He hangs up his coat and cap, and takes off his felt shoes, and sets them neatly side by side.

He climbs the stairs, one step at a time, and the old wood creaks in a friendly way. In the bedroom, the curtains are drawn, and the room is dim and cool. The bed is wide, and soft, and made, with a heavy quilt turned back, waiting for him as it always does.

He sits on the edge, and unbuttons his cuffs, and lets his arms rest. He is pleasantly tired, in the way one is tired after good work, a tiredness that feels like a warm weight, settling over him from the shoulders down to the heels.

He lies back, and draws up the quilt, and rests his head on the pillow. It takes the weight of his head, as the dough took the weight of his hands, with a soft, yielding sigh. Through the curtains, a thin, grey light creeps across the ceiling, and the sound of the rain is almost gone.

Somewhere in the town, an alarm clock rings, and a door opens, and the first footsteps sound on the cobblestones. The day is beginning for everyone else. But in this small, dim room, the night is only now arriving, and it arrives softly, like a cat on a windowsill.

Tomas breathes in, and out. His hands lie open on the quilt. He thinks of the bakery, empty and warm, with its twenty golden loaves. He thinks of the people who will carry them home. He thinks of the rain, and the oven, and the old, steady clock.

His breathing slows, and lengthens. His thoughts drift apart like the steam from a cup of tea, thinning, and rising, and fading into the air. There is nothing left to knead, or to shape, or to watch. There is only the soft, deep dark behind his eyelids, and the quiet.

And somewhere in the middle of that quiet, Tomas falls asleep. His face is calm. His breath is even. The smell of bread still clings faintly to his sleeves, and the morning goes on without him, bright and busy, and he does not mind at all.

Now it is your turn to do just the same. Let your breath find its own pace. Let your arms and legs grow heavy, as if the bed were holding every part of you. Let your jaw rest, and your brow soften, and your thoughts rise like steam from a warm cup.

Imagine, if you like, that you are lying in a small room, with the curtains drawn, and the scent of fresh bread drifting somewhere nearby. Each breath is a slow, soft wave. Each wave carries a little more of the day away, and leaves behind a little more calm.

There is nothing left to do. The loaves are baked, and the oven is cooling, and the town is waking gently, a long way off. You are warm, and you are safe, and the whole of the quiet morning is yours to rest in.

You can rest now.

Goodnight.
